docs.title: Collision detection methodology
docs.text: Collision detection is split into a broad phase and a precise phase. Meshes and boundary representations (BReps) follow separate pipelines; the implementation never converts or compares mixed representations.

docs.title: Current capability
docs.text:
The public queries are:

  • is_mesh_mesh_collision_fast
  • is_brep_brep_collision_fast
  • is_mesh_mesh_collision
  • is_brep_brep_collision
  • Element.is_collision(..., precision="fast")
  • Element.is_collision(..., precision="precise")
  • Model.collision_candidates() and Model.collisions(...)

Fast queries are conservative. A False result means the two geometry bounds are separated. A True result means only that their bounds overlap, so the underlying geometries can still be disjoint. This distinction is intentional: the fast query is suitable for pruning, not for proving geometric intersection.

Precise mesh collision is implemented by Coal. Precise BRep collision is implemented for COMPAS OCC BReps using their native Open CASCADE shapes. Other BRep backends fail explicitly rather than being tessellated or silently routed through the mesh pipeline.

The exported is_polyhedron_polyhedron_collision function remains an unimplemented legacy placeholder. Polyhedron collision semantics are outside the mesh/BRep milestone documented here.

docs.title: Precise mesh-surface collision
docs.text:
is_mesh_mesh_collision converts each COMPAS mesh to a Coal BVHModelOBBRSS:

  1. Faces are triangulated by Mesh.to_vertices_and_faces(triangulated=True) without mutating the source mesh.
  2. Empty meshes, non-finite coordinates, and zero-area triangles are rejected.
  3. Vertices and triangle indices are copied into Coal's native containers.
  4. Coal builds an OBB/RSS triangle hierarchy and performs the narrow-phase query.

The function classifies intersections between mesh surfaces. A closed mesh entirely contained in another closed mesh returns False if their surfaces do not meet. General COMPAS meshes may be open and do not intrinsically define a solid interior, so solid-volume overlap is intentionally not inferred.

Touching counts as collision. Coal contact depths for triangle meshes do not reliably distinguish every coplanar face or edge contact from surface penetration. For that reason, precise calls with include_touching=False raise NotImplementedError instead of returning an ambiguous classification.

Positive tolerance is passed to Coal as its collision security margin. This causes separated surfaces within the requested distance to count as colliding. Negative tolerances are rejected.

Coal is optional for ordinary use. Install the collision extra or the conda package when precise mesh queries are needed:

pip install "compas_model[collision]"
# or
conda install -c conda-forge coal

Standalone is_mesh_mesh_collision calls prepare both Coal triangle hierarchies for that query. Elements cache their prepared hierarchy, so Model.collisions(precision="precise") prepares each participating element at most once and reuses it across candidate pairs and subsequent calls.

docs.title: Precise BRep collision
docs.text:
is_brep_brep_collision operates directly on the native shapes stored by compas_occ.brep.OCCBrep; it does not tessellate them. Before a query, Open CASCADE's shape analyzer rejects null and invalid topology.

When touching is included, BRepExtrema_DistShapeShape computes the minimum distance between the two shapes. A distance less than or equal to tolerance is a collision. Intersecting boundaries and solid containment both produce zero distance, so this path detects containment as well as contact. The effective comparison tolerance is never smaller than Open CASCADE's Precision::Confusion() resolution; this absorbs kernel-level floating-point residuals at analytically tangent curved surfaces.

When touching is excluded, both BReps must be solids. The implementation computes their Boolean common and requires a positive-volume solid result. This rejects face, edge, and vertex contact while accepting penetration and containment. Positive tolerance cannot currently be combined with excluded touching: a non-negative distance cannot express penetration depth for arbitrary BReps, so this combination raises NotImplementedError rather than guessing.

Kernel failures are reported as RuntimeError, and unsupported BRep backends as TypeError. Install the BRep extra or the conda package for precise BRep queries:

pip install "compas_model[brep]"
# or
conda install -c conda-forge compas_occ

docs.title: Bounding boxes and tolerances
docs.text:
Mesh bounds are computed from every mesh vertex. Mesh faces and topology do not affect the fast result. BRep bounds come from Brep.aabb, allowing the active geometry backend to account for extrema of curved faces instead of using only BRep vertices.

Two axis-aligned bounds intersect when their closed intervals overlap on all three coordinate axes. By default, boundary contact counts as intersection. With include_touching=False, every axis must overlap by more than tolerance. With include_touching=True, gaps no larger than tolerance are accepted. Negative tolerances are rejected.

Backend-computed BRep bounds may include a small numerical padding. For example, Open CASCADE expands bounds to preserve robustness. Therefore, include_touching=False describes contact between the computed AABBs, not an exact classification of contact between ideal BRep surfaces. This can create a false positive, which is valid for a conservative broad phase.

docs.title: Model BVH
docs.text:
The model spatial index is a purpose-built binary bounding volume hierarchy (BVH), independent of the COMPAS Tree data structure. Construction proceeds as follows:

  1. Wrap each element in a record containing its key, centroid, payload, and bounding points.
  2. Compute the node bound around all records.
  3. Select the node-box axis with the largest dimension.
  4. Sort record centroids along that axis and split at the median.
  5. Repeat until leafsize or max_depth stops subdivision.

This median split gives deterministic, reasonably balanced trees. It is not a surface-area heuristic and does not claim to produce an optimal hierarchy. Oriented nodes use a principal-component box, which is likewise not guaranteed to be the minimum-volume oriented box.

Candidate generation traverses two trees together. Non-overlapping node pairs are discarded. When both nodes are leaves, their object pairs are emitted; otherwise the node with the larger bounding-box volume is descended first. Self-comparison removes identity pairs and duplicate unordered pairs.

Model.collisions() normally uses this BVH pruning before dispatching each pair to its representation-specific query. A positive tolerance can make separated element bounds count as colliding; because the current BVH traversal has no inflated-bound mode, the model method exhaustively checks element pairs in that case. This preserves correctness at the cost of broad-phase performance.

docs.title: Cache behavior
docs.text:
The model caches its BVH, and mesh elements cache their prepared Coal collision models. OCC BReps already retain their native kernel shapes, so no second BRep collision cache is created. Adding or removing elements invalidates the spatial index. Replacing or transforming element geometry, transforming the model, adding a feature, or adding a modifier invalidates derived geometry, prepared collision models, and spatial indices. Invalidation currently covers all model elements because hierarchical transformations and modifiers can propagate changes.

Direct mutation inside a mesh or direct mutation of the exposed feature list cannot be observed automatically. Callers should replace the element geometry, use the provided mutation methods, or explicitly trigger a model-level change after such mutation. Dependency-aware invalidation may make the conservative model-wide reset more selective in the future.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
The automated tests cover overlapping, separated, touching, nearly tangent, tolerance-expanded, contained, curved, small-volume, large-coordinate, degenerate, empty, and invalid inputs. They also verify polygon triangulation, unique self-collision pairs, dual-tree traversal, mixed AABB/OBB traversal, prepared-model reuse and invalidation, and explicit failures for unsupported precise semantics. CI imports both optional backends explicitly so these tests cannot silently disappear through dependency-based skips.

Run the checks in the development environment with:

conda run -n model-dev pytest
conda run -n model-dev pyright
conda run -n model-dev ruff check src tests
conda run -n model-dev mkdocs build --strict

See References for the underlying algorithms and backends.

docs.title: Contact detection audit
docs.text: This page records the behavior and limitations of the contact-interface code as of October 2026. Resolved audit items are documented alongside the remaining limitations so the implementation can be checked independently.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
Contact detection currently finds planar face-to-face interface regions. It is distinct from collision detection:

  • collision detection answers whether two representations overlap, touch, or lie within a distance tolerance;
  • contact detection attempts to construct one or more oriented planar regions suitable for downstream equilibrium calculations;
  • solid penetration, containment, edge contact, and vertex contact do not by themselves define a planar contact interface.

Mesh and BRep inputs follow separate paths and are never mixed.

docs.title: Current mesh methodology
docs.text:
mesh_mesh_contacts compares every face of the first mesh with every face of the second mesh. Faces whose normals are not opposite are discarded. Each remaining pair is fitted to a shared plane, projected to that plane, and intersected as PlanarRegion geometry using Shapely. Every connected result becomes a separate Contact, holes are preserved, and regions smaller than minimum_area are discarded.

This is an exhaustive quadratic face-pair search. It does not yet use Coal's triangle hierarchy or the model BVH. It is intended for polygonal planar interfaces, not arbitrary curved or penetrating mesh surfaces.

Mesh faces are used as stored and are not triangulated by contact detection. If a polygon's vertices deviate from its best-fit plane by more than the absolute tolerance, that face pair produces no contact rather than aborting the complete search. This is particularly relevant to rounded or low-precision OBJ data: preserving nonplanar quads can produce fewer contacts than triangulating those quads into independently planar faces.

docs.title: Current BRep methodology
docs.text:
brep_brep_contacts first calls the active BRep backend's overlap method. For COMPAS OCC this meshes both shapes and uses BRepExtrema_ShapeProximity to obtain candidate faces. Candidate face sets are then cross-compared, filtered by opposite polygon normals, converted to PlanarRegion geometry with their face holes, and intersected with Shapely.

Therefore, “precise BRep contact interface” currently means a planar polygon intersection computed from selected BRep face boundaries. Candidate selection is tessellation-based and controlled by deflection; it is not an exact OCC face-face Boolean operation.

docs.title: Verified baseline
docs.text: Automated tests verify mesh and OCC BRep box interfaces in all axis directions, partial face overlaps, corner-offset overlaps, and rejection of edge-only contact. The BRep tests had previously been disabled and are now active.

docs.title: Geometry-result model
docs.text: The previous single-polygon assumption has been removed. Polygon, MultiPolygon, and polygonal GeometryCollection intersections now produce a list of connected planar regions. Contact stores one authoritative PlanarRegion; its size is net area, and its BRep and constrained Delaunay mesh both preserve holes. Shapely 2.1 or newer is required for the constrained triangulation.

docs.title: Candidate generation
docs.text:
Model.compute_contacts uses ElementBVH.nearby_elements. For each element, the query expands its axis-aligned bounding box by the requested absolute tolerance in all six directions and traverses the cached model BVH. This is a conservative broad phase: it may return false positives, especially when BVH leaves contain multiple elements, but it cannot reject two geometries whose Euclidean separation is at most the tolerance. Every unordered pair is evaluated once, in model insertion order, which makes contact orientation deterministic. Mixed Mesh/BRep pairs are skipped rather than dispatched to an unsupported algorithm.

The expansion is absolute and independent of element size. In particular, small elements separated by a valid tolerance are no longer missed by the old relative 20% search box. A negative tolerance is rejected before the BVH is queried.

The mesh function performs all face-pair comparisons. The BRep function uses backend proximity candidates, but loses face-pair correspondence and cross-compares the two returned face sets.

docs.title: Tolerances and validation
docs.text: One tolerance currently controls broad-phase proximity, face coplanarity, and projection deviation. These are different numerical decisions and may become explicit parameters in a future tolerance policy. Angular opposition uses a fixed relative dot-product tolerance. Negative tolerances and minimum areas are rejected; backend failures are not normalized into a common exception type.

docs.title: Model and interaction-graph updates
docs.text:
Model recomputation is transactional with respect to geometry computation: all candidate contacts are calculated before the interaction graph is changed. If one calculation raises, no graph contacts or edges are changed. Successful recomputation replaces derived contacts and clears stale results, including pairs that are no longer broad-phase candidates.

Two edge attributes record provenance. contacts_computed identifies a contact value managed by recomputation; contact_edge identifies an interaction edge created solely because a contact was found. A stale contact-only edge is deleted. An explicit user-created edge is preserved with contacts=None, and a generated edge is also preserved if it has acquired modifiers. Contact values without contacts_computed=True are treated as user-authored and are not cleared merely because their pair falls outside the current candidate set.

docs.title: Recommended implementation order
docs.text:
1. Add curved, invalid, duplicate-interface, and deterministic-orientation tests before exposing contact interfaces in the custom viewer.
  2. Investigate retaining BRep face-pair correspondence from the OCC proximity query instead of cross-comparing candidate face sets.
  3. Separate broad-phase, coplanarity, and projection tolerances if real-world model scales demonstrate that one tolerance is insufficient.

This order intentionally overlaps with the planned section infrastructure: sections and contact interfaces both need robust oriented planar regions with multiple components and holes.

docs.title: Geometry foundation
docs.text:
The first infrastructure step is implemented as compas_model.geometry.PlanarRegion and intersection_planar_region_planar_region:

  • a region contains one oriented exterior and zero or more oppositely oriented holes;
  • area is net area, with holes subtracted;
  • regions are validated for coplanarity and valid polygonal topology;
  • intersections return a deterministic list of connected regions;
  • Polygon, MultiPolygon, and polygonal GeometryCollection results are supported, while boundary-only results are discarded;
  • result frames follow the first input, preserving source-to-target contact orientation;
  • regions support COMPAS serialization, transformations, AABBs, and OBBs.

Both contact algorithms and Contact now use this primitive. Compatibility accessors still expose the exterior polygon, points, holes, frame, mesh, brep, and size, while Contact.geometry returns the complete planar region.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
The model-level migration is covered by tests for absolute tolerance on small elements, unique BVH candidates, replacement of changed interfaces, removal of stale generated edges, preservation of explicit edges, and invalid options. Run the focused checks with:

pytest tests/test_algorithms_bvh.py tests/test_model.py tests/test_algorithms_contacts.py

docs.text: COMPAS Model requires Python 3.12 or newer. The project is continuously tested with Python 3.12, 3.13, and 3.14.

docs.title: Full
docs.text:
conda create -n model python=3.12 compas compas_occ compas_viewer

docs.title: References
docs.text: This list records sources that inform implemented collision functionality or a clearly identified planned precise phase. A citation does not imply that every optimization described by the source is implemented.

docs.title: Implemented foundations
docs.text:
1. Gottschalk, S., Lin, M. C., and Manocha, D. (1996). “OBBTree: A Hierarchical Structure for Rapid Interference Detection.” Proceedings of SIGGRAPH 1996, 171–180. Project publication page. Background for bounding-volume hierarchies and oriented bounding boxes. The current tree uses median splitting, not the paper's complete construction.

  2. Ericson, C. (2005). Real-Time Collision Detection. Morgan Kaufmann. Publisher page. Reference for separating-axis tests, bounding volumes, and BVH traversal.

  3. COMPAS Association. “Brep API.” COMPAS documentation. Defines the backend-neutral BRep interface used by the fast query.

  4. Open CASCADE Technology. “Modeling Algorithms: Boolean Operations.” OCCT documentation. Documents the common-volume operation used to distinguish solid penetration from boundary-only contact.

  5. Open CASCADE Technology. “BRepExtrema_DistShapeShape Class Reference.” OCCT API documentation. Documents the native-shape minimum-distance query used for BRep contact, containment, and tolerance-aware proximity.

  6. Open CASCADE Technology. “BRepExtrema_ShapeProximity Class Reference.” OCCT API documentation. Documents the tessellation-based candidate-face proximity query used by the current COMPAS OCC contact path.

  7. Shapely contributors. “MultiPolygon.” Shapely documentation. Documents the multi-component result type that planar contact intersection must support.

  8. Pan, J., Chitta, S., and Manocha, D. (2012). “FCL: A General Purpose Library for Collision and Proximity Queries.” IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation, 3859–3866. Author-hosted paper. Foundation for the triangle BVH collision backend.

  9. Carpentier, J., Montaut, L., and the Coal contributors. “Coal: An Extension of the Flexible Collision Library.” Project repository. Backend used for precise mesh-surface collision and tolerance margins.

  10. Shapely contributors. “line_merge” and “unary_union.” Shapely line merging documentation and union documentation. These topology operations assemble welded mesh-plane segments and combine coplanar triangle polygons in the mesh section backend.

  11. Open CASCADE Technology. “BRepAlgoAPI_Section Class Reference.” OCCT API documentation. Documents the native plane/shape intersection operation used by the BRep section backend.

  12. Open CASCADE Technology. “BOPAlgo_Splitter Class Reference.” OCCT API documentation. Documents the native splitting operation wrapped by COMPAS OCC for retained BRep half-spaces.

  13. Mapbox contributors. “Earcut.” Algorithm repository and Python bindings. Provides the modified ear-clipping implementation used for triangulating polygonal render faces, including faces with holes.

  14. Open CASCADE Technology. “BRepMesh_IncrementalMesh Class Reference.” OCCT API documentation. Documents the native BRep face tessellation used through COMPAS OCC's to_viewmesh infrastructure.

docs.title: Planned precise phase
docs.text: 1. Möller, T., and Trumbore, B. (1997). “Fast, Minimum Storage Ray-Triangle Intersection.” Journal of Graphics Tools, 2(1), 21–28. Author-hosted paper. The existing ray-triangle primitive follows this method and can support triangle-level queries.

docs.title: Sectioning infrastructure
docs.text: Sectioning uses the same oriented PlanarRegion geometry as contact detection. The backend-independent result model and separate Mesh and native OCC BRep backends are implemented. Representations are never mixed during sectioning.

docs.title: Oriented-plane convention
docs.text:
A SectionResult stores the cutting plane as a Frame. The frame Z axis is the plane normal and establishes the two half-spaces. For a point p and frame origin o, signed distance is computed as:

(p - o) dot frame.zaxis

The classification rules are:

  • distance greater than tolerance: front;
  • distance smaller than -tolerance: behind;
  • absolute distance less than or equal to tolerance: coplanar;
  • geometry spanning both half-spaces, or containing points on the plane and on one side of it: intersecting.

This convention is independent of the Mesh or BRep backend. Reversing the frame Z axis swaps front and behind.

docs.title: Sections versus clips
docs.text:
Sectioning and clipping are deliberately separate operations:

  • a section contains only geometry on the cutting plane: closed faces as PlanarRegion objects and their outlines, plus any open intersection curves;
  • a clip contains the section together with the source geometry retained in the negative (behind) half-space.

This distinction keeps a section independent of decisions about which side of an object to retain. A clip always keeps the side where signed distance is negative. Reverse the frame Z axis to keep the other side.

The public backend functions follow the same distinction:

  • section_mesh and section_brep return SectionElementResult;
  • clip_mesh and clip_brep return ClipElementResult.

docs.title: Result model
docs.text:
SectionElementResult stores the result for one source element:

  • source element GUID and representation (mesh or brep);
  • spatial classification;
  • zero or more closed PlanarRegion section components;
  • zero or more open intersection polylines;

Its outlines accessor contains the exterior and hole boundaries of every closed region, followed by the open intersection curves.

ClipElementResult composes a SectionElementResult with an optional snapshot of geometry retained behind the plane. Geometry that is wholly behind the plane is retained without trimming. Geometry wholly in front of or coplanar with the plane has no retained geometry.

Retained geometry must match the declared representation. Constructor inputs are copied so later mutations of model geometry cannot silently change an existing section result.

SectionResult stores the cutting frame, tolerance, and ordered section records. It validates that every section region and open curve lies on the cutting plane within the recorded tolerance. Convenience accessors collect regions, outlines, open curves, and records by classification without changing their deterministic input order.

ClipResult stores the same cutting frame and tolerance, ordered clip records, and the capping choice. Its section accessor provides the corresponding geometry-only SectionResult, while its geometry accessor collects retained objects.

All four result types support COMPAS serialization and transformations. Constructor inputs are copied, and a transformation moves the plane, section geometry, and retained geometry together. This snapshot behavior prevents a later mutation of source model geometry from changing an existing result.

docs.title: Mesh methodology
docs.text:
intersection_mesh_plane obtains a triangulated view of the input without modifying it. Triangle edges are classified by signed distance, crossing points are projected to the cutting plane, and endpoints are welded in plane-local XY coordinates using the requested tolerance. Shapely merges the resulting line network. Closed rings are classified by nesting depth to construct disconnected PlanarRegion components and holes; unclosed chains become Polyline results. Coplanar triangles are unioned as planar polygons. A completely coplanar mesh is therefore classified coplanar and can still produce regions.

section_mesh stops after producing the planar result. clip_mesh additionally calls clip_mesh_halfspace, which uses polygon half-space clipping on every original mesh face and keeps the negative half-space. When the input is closed and cap=True, all unfiltered section regions are triangulated and joined to the clipped boundaries. Consequently, minimum_area filters the reported regions without accidentally leaving a requested clipped solid open. Open input meshes are never capped.

The line and polygon operations are tolerance-based. Features or gaps at or below the welding tolerance may merge. The result may contain conservative topological simplification at that scale. Clipping does not repair invalid, self-intersecting, nonmanifold, or inconsistently oriented input meshes.

For a tangent cut, the element is intersecting, its boundary region is reported, and the nonempty retained side is an unchanged geometry snapshot. The zero-thickness opposite side is omitted. Entirely-behind geometry is always copied into a clip result.

docs.title: BRep methodology
docs.text:
intersection_brep_plane requires a native COMPAS OCC BRep. Open CASCADE's BRepAlgoAPI_Section computes the section edges against an infinite planar face. Those edges remain exact in the backend result, but PlanarRegion boundaries are polygonal by design. Each native edge is therefore sampled with curve_samples points and passed through the same plane-local welding, ring nesting, and open-chain reconstruction used by mesh section curves. Increasing curve_samples improves curved-region area accuracy without changing the native section operation.

section_brep stops after producing the planar result. clip_brep uses OCC shape splitting and retains the negative half-space; reversing the plane retains the positive side. The resulting solids are natively capped by OCC. Uncapped intersected BRep output is currently unsupported and raises NotImplementedError rather than silently returning capped geometry. A wholly behind BRep does not require splitting and can therefore be returned regardless of the capping option.

Half-space classification combines native section existence with BRep topological points and a surface tessellation. The section and trimmed solids remain native operations, but classification of pathological or very small curved features is therefore limited by backend tessellation. The requested tolerance affects signed-distance classification, coplanarity, endpoint welding, and region validation; it does not expand the infinite plane into a thick slab for the native OCC section operation.

Tangent sections are classified intersecting. A tangent edge or face may produce a region, while an isolated tangent point has no polygonal or polyline representation and therefore produces no section geometry. Entirely coplanar faces are classified coplanar.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
The section and clip contracts are tested independently for empty and ordered results, signed-distance classification, regions with holes, outlines, open curves, retained geometry, snapshot behavior, serialization, transformations, plane validation, tangent cases, whole-half-space cases, and invalid options:

pytest tests/test_geometry_section.py
pytest tests/test_geometry_mesh_section.py
pytest tests/test_geometry_brep_section.py

docs.title: Model viewer infrastructure
docs.text: The model viewer integration separates domain geometry from render geometry. Elements keep their original Mesh or BRep representation for modelling and precise computations. RenderGeometry is a backend-neutral, CPU-side snapshot containing arrays suitable for interactive rendering; it is not serialized as part of an element and is not used for collision, contact, section, or clip calculations.

docs.title: Face and boundary representation
docs.text:
Filled surfaces and visible boundaries are stored independently:

  • vertices and triangles describe filled faces;
  • line_vertices contains explicit pairs of visible boundary endpoints;
  • point_vertices contains optional display points.

This distinction prevents the internal diagonals introduced by triangulation from appearing as model edges.

For a Mesh, every original face is triangulated for filled rendering, while the line buffer is built only from Mesh.edges(). Concave polygon faces are therefore rendered with triangles without displaying their triangulation diagonals.

For a BRep, render_geometry_from_brep uses the backend's to_viewmesh operation. With COMPAS OCC this reuses Open CASCADE's face tessellation and the separately sampled topological edge polylines. The tessellation approximates curved surfaces according to the backend's linear and angular deflection, but the displayed line buffer follows BRep edge boundaries rather than triangle edges.

ElementObject computes this representation once when the scene object is created and supplies it directly to COMPAS Viewer's buffer-building methods.

docs.title: Model viewer controller
docs.text:
ModelViewer is the integration point for displaying an entire model. It owns one shared RenderGeometryCache and one shared RenderSettings instance, adds the model and its elements to COMPAS Viewer, and indexes the resulting concrete ElementObject instances by element GUID.

from compas_model.viewer import ModelViewer

controller = ModelViewer(model)
controller.select([element], clear=True)
controller.hide([other_element])
controller.refresh(element)
controller.show_viewer()

The controller traverses Model.tree and creates the same parent-child relationships in the COMPAS scene. The model tree remains authoritative; no second hierarchy or intermediate element-view objects are created. Scene objects can be retrieved with object_for_element or object_for_guid for tree widgets and property inspectors.

refresh updates one object's render geometry, while refresh_all checks all objects against their element geometry revisions. Selection and visibility operate directly on the concrete scene objects. On Python 3.14, automatic viewer construction applies the local COMPAS Viewer 2.0.1 configuration compatibility patch before instantiating the viewer.

docs.title: Model navigation projections
docs.text:
By default, ModelViewer replaces COMPAS Viewer's generic scene form with a ModelNavigationForm containing four views of the same data:

  • Hierarchy follows the authoritative parent-child structure in Model.tree.
  • Collections shows named, potentially overlapping element sets and an Uncollected branch.
  • Types groups element references by their concrete Python class.
  • Interactions projects interaction-graph edges as element pairs, with computed planar contact regions and modifiers below them.

These are transient Qt projections, not additional model containers. Element items store GUIDs and resolve through ModelViewer; interaction items store graph-edge and region indices and resolve through Model.graph. Consequently, changing a projection never changes model ownership, group membership, or the interaction graph. Rebuilding the tabs with update(refresh=True) reflects structural changes made through the model API.

Group and Collection intentionally have different semantics. A Group is an element in Model.tree: it expresses assembly or containment, has one hierarchical parent, and may own child elements. A Collection is model data outside that hierarchy. It stores ordered element GUID references, can overlap other collections, and has no geometry, transformation, BVH entry, or interaction-graph node.

facade = model.add_collection("Facade", attributes={"discipline": "architecture"})
phase_1 = model.add_collection("Phase 1")

facade.add_elements([wall_a, wall_b, window])
phase_1.add_elements([wall_a, column, slab])

Collections are serialized with the model. Removing an element removes its membership from every collection; removing a collection does not remove its elements. collections_for_element resolves overlapping membership.

The element projections support multiple selection. Tree selections update the ElementObject.is_selected flags through the controller, while update() synchronizes viewport selections across all projections. The visibility column updates ElementObject.show. Changing a branch checkbox applies the same state to all descendant element objects.

Synthetic projection headings are bulk controls rather than decorative labels. Selecting a heading such as MeshElement selects every element referenced by that type branch. Its visibility checkbox shows or hides the complete branch and displays a partial state when member visibility is mixed. The same behavior applies to collection headings and the synthetic Uncollected heading.

Selecting a contact pair or region selects both incident elements in the viewport and sends the contact selection to the inspector. Contacts remain derived interaction data: they are deliberately not inserted into Model.tree. The interaction view currently exposes computed contacts; other edge payloads and transient collision-query result sets can be added as separate projections without conflating them with persistent element hierarchy.

Computed contacts are rendered by a ContactLayer. Every planar contact region has its own scene object and picking identifier; contact meshes are not joined. A region can therefore be selected either in the viewport or in the Interactions tree. The Show column controls one region, all regions on an element-pair edge, or the complete contact layer through the All interactions row. Viewport selection is synchronized back to the tree and selection inspector when COMPAS Viewer refreshes its sidebar.

This region-level representation intentionally trades a larger scene-object count for independently verifiable picking and visibility. Applications that only need the model geometry can construct ModelViewer(..., show_contacts=False); the contact objects still exist for inspection but start hidden.

An optional selection_changed callback receives the selected elements and is the intended integration point for the element properties and attributes inspector. Applications that provide a different UI can construct ModelViewer(..., install_tree=False) and use the controller lookup and selection APIs directly.

docs.title: Selection inspector
docs.text:
ElementInspector adds a read-only Selection tab to the COMPAS Viewer sidebar. Despite its compatibility-preserving class name, it displays both element and contact selections. For a contact selection it reports the two incident elements, selected region count, total area, and each region's area, boundary-point count, hole count, and triangulated face count.

For a single selected element it reports:

  • identity, parent, child count, selection, and visibility;
  • element parameters exposed through serialized Element.__data__, excluding infrastructure fields such as transformation, features, and material links;
  • semantic attributes stored on the element's model-tree node;
  • assigned material type, GUID, and serialized properties;
  • source Mesh or BRep topology counts, geometry revision, and generated render buffer counts.

For multiple elements the inspector reports the selection count, type distribution, and visible count. inspect_elements produces the same structured InspectorSection data independently of the Qt widget, making the display logic directly testable and reusable by other interfaces.

The inspector deliberately starts read-only. Editing arbitrary serialized values would bypass element validation and geometry invalidation; editable controls should therefore be added later through explicit parameter metadata and setters rather than generic attribute assignment. Applications can disable automatic installation with ModelViewer(..., install_inspector=False).

docs.title: Cross-vault example
docs.text:
examples/contact_detection/cross_vault_model_viewer.py demonstrates the complete infrastructure with the 184-block cross vault. It computes the block contacts, organizes blocks into four overlapping-capable spatial collections, exposes contact counts as tree-node attributes, preselects the block with the most contact regions, and displays every contact interface as an independently selectable red region.

python examples/contact_detection/cross_vault_model_viewer.py

Use the collection checkboxes to hide an entire quadrant, compare the hierarchy, collection, and type projections, select contact pairs or regions in the Interactions tab, and inspect their computed geometry in the Selection tab. The computational setup can be verified without opening a window:

python examples/contact_detection/cross_vault_model_viewer.py --no-viewer

docs.title: Units and approximation quality
docs.text:
Model.unit records whether coordinate values are metres (M) or millimetres (MM). It is serialized with the model. Changing the metadata reinterprets coordinate values; it never scales existing geometry.

RenderSettings derives linear deflection from the diagonal of each element's axis-aligned bounding box and then clamps it to physical limits converted into model units:

linear deflection = clamp(relative deflection × diagonal,
                          physical minimum,
                          physical maximum)
Quality Relative deflection Physical minimum Physical maximum Angular deflection draft 1e-2 × diagonal 0.1 mm 20 mm 0.20 rad standard 1e-3 × diagonal 0.01 mm 5 mm 0.10 rad high 1e-4 × diagonal 0.001 mm 1 mm 0.05 rad

For example, a one-metre object at standard quality uses a one-millimetre deflection: 0.001 in a metre model or 1.0 in a millimetre model. A ten-metre object uses the five-millimetre physical maximum rather than an unbounded relative error. Degenerate and extremely small objects use the physical minimum. Translation does not affect the diagonal, so large global coordinates do not coarsen tessellation; algorithms operating far from the origin may nevertheless require local-coordinate conditioning for numerical robustness.

Angular deflection is unitless. The default Mesh cleanup tolerance is separate from visual tessellation and represents the same physical distance: 1e-9 metres or 1e-6 millimetres. Explicit tolerance and deflection values are interpreted in model units and override the presets.

An ElementObject with implicit settings adopts its model's unit and tracks later metadata changes when its render geometry is refreshed. Explicit settings must use the same unit as the model, preventing an accidental metre/millimetre mismatch.

Every element has a runtime-only geometry_revision. Existing element and model invalidation paths increment this revision whenever they clear derived geometry. The revision is deliberately not serialized: deserialized elements start a new runtime cache lifecycle.

RenderGeometryCache keys entries by element GUID and verifies all of the following before returning a hit:

  • the Python element identity is unchanged;
  • geometry_revision is unchanged;
  • Mesh triangulation and BRep tessellation settings are unchanged.

This prevents a different element carrying the same GUID, stale derived geometry, or a different tessellation quality from reusing an incompatible render snapshot. ElementObject owns the resulting snapshot directly; there is no separate element-view state or duplicated render-geometry reference. Explicit invalidation is also available. Direct in-place mutation of the Mesh or BRep stored inside an element cannot be observed by the element setter and therefore requires explicit cache invalidation; assigning the geometry property or using model/element transformations updates the revision automatically.

The current model invalidation policy is deliberately conservative: a geometry change can affect descendants, interactions, and modifiers, so it increments the revisions of all elements in the model. The cache still avoids rebuilding anything until a view is refreshed, but a complete model refresh may rebuild all element render geometry after such a change. More selective dependency tracking can be added later without changing the cache contract. A future model-viewer controller can index the concrete element objects by GUID for tree selection and visibility control without introducing another state owner.

docs.title: Ear-clipping methodology
docs.text:
triangulate_polygon_earcut provides reusable triangulation for a planar exterior ring with optional holes. It performs the following steps:

  1. Remove a repeated closing point, consecutive duplicates, and collinear points within the requested tolerance.
  2. Compute the exterior Newell normal and project all rings by dropping its dominant coordinate.
  3. Reject degenerate or topologically invalid projected polygons with Shapely.
  4. Triangulate the projected rings with Mapbox Earcut.
  5. Restore the exterior ring's original winding to the generated triangles.
  6. Compare the summed triangle area with the validated polygon area and reject incomplete output.

Earcut is designed to return useful results for practical polygon data and is not a formal guarantee for arbitrary invalid or self-intersecting input. The explicit validity and area checks prevent such output from silently entering render buffers. Projection assumes that input rings describe one planar face; it does not repair materially nonplanar faces.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
The numerical triangulation and render-buffer topology can be checked without starting a graphical interface:

pytest tests/test_geometry_triangulation.py
pytest tests/test_viewer_rendergeometry.py
pytest tests/test_viewer_viewstate.py
pytest tests/test_viewer_controller.py
pytest tests/test_viewer_treeform.py

The tests cover concavity, winding, holes, duplicate and collinear vertices, degenerate and self-intersecting input, invalid indices, hidden triangulation diagonals, native OCC view-mesh boundaries, model hierarchy mapping, selection, visibility, cache reuse, refresh, units, and empty models.

docs.title: Visually verifying collision detection
docs.text:
The collision examples combine executable assertions with an interactive COMPAS Viewer scene. Green geometry participates in a precise collision, amber geometry illustrates boundary-only or broad-phase-only results, red geometry is separated, and grey geometry has no reported collision.

Install the visualization and collision backends first:

pip install -e ".[viz,collision,brep]"

Run the examples from the repository root:

python examples/collision_detection/mesh_overlap.py
python examples/collision_detection/brep_boundary_cases.py
python examples/collision_detection/model_broad_vs_precise.py

The examples demonstrate:

  1. A simple mesh overlap for which fast and precise checks agree.
  2. Penetrating, face-touching, and narrowly separated native OCC BReps.
  3. A model-level comparison in which the fast AABB query reports containment as a candidate while precise mesh-surface collision correctly rejects it.

Each script checks its expected results before opening the viewer. For CI, headless machines, or quick terminal verification, append --no-viewer:

python examples/collision_detection/model_broad_vs_precise.py --no-viewer

The colors and labels are explanatory output only. The collision result is computed before visualization; the viewer does not participate in detection.

docs.title: Visually verifying contact detection
docs.text:
The contact examples render source geometry transparently and draw the computed contact regions in opaque red. This makes the actual output geometry, rather than only a Boolean result, visually inspectable.

Run them from the repository root:

python examples/contact_detection/model_boundary_cases.py
python examples/contact_detection/disconnected_regions.py
python examples/contact_detection/brep_hole.py
python examples/contact_detection/cross_vault.py

The scenes verify three distinct parts of the implementation:

  1. model_boundary_cases.py compares exact face contact, a small gap accepted by an absolute tolerance, and a gap outside that tolerance. It exercises the model BVH candidate search and graph-managed contacts.
  2. disconnected_regions.py intersects a U-shaped mesh face with a crossing face. The result must be two independent Contact objects of area 0.5.
  3. brep_hole.py computes a planar OCC BRep interface whose exterior area is 16 and hole area is 4. The displayed contact mesh must retain the hole and have net area 12.
  4. cross_vault.py loads all 184 named block objects from data/cross_vault.obj, builds a model, and runs the tolerance-aware contact workflow while preserving the source polygonal faces: the loaded meshes contain 1248 quads and 16 triangles. The three-decimal OBJ export contains slightly nonplanar quads. Such faces are not valid planar contact operands and are skipped rather than triangulated. With tolerance and minimum area both set to 0.01, the current verified result is therefore 257 contacting block pairs and 257 contact regions. The model viewer gives every contact region its own selectable scene object.

As with the collision examples, every script asserts its numerical and topological expectations before opening the viewer. Append --no-viewer for headless verification:

python examples/contact_detection/model_boundary_cases.py --no-viewer

These examples visualize planar contact interfaces. They do not imply that edge-only contact, vertex-only contact, penetration, or arbitrary curved surface intersections produce a contact region.

docs.title: Visually verifying sections and clips
docs.text:
The sectioning examples place three cases side by side: a geometry-only section, a retained negative-half-space clip, and a more complex clip whose section contains a hole. Source geometry is translucent grey, computed section faces are red, and retained clip geometry is blue or green.

Run the Mesh and native OCC BRep variants from the repository root:

python examples/sectioning/mesh_sections_and_clips.py
python examples/sectioning/brep_sections_and_clips.py

The Mesh example verifies polygonal intersection reconstruction, capped half-space clipping, and preservation of a section hole. The BRep example shows that the displayed curved section face is sampled into a polygonal PlanarRegion, while the retained half-sphere and hollow box are exact native OCC clipping results.

The frame Z axis points toward the discarded front side in every case. The clip retains negative signed distances (behind); reversing the Z axis would retain the other half. The translucent full source shown beside or around a clip is explanatory context added by the example and is not part of the returned clip geometry.

Both scripts assert expected areas, holes, and retained volumes before opening the viewer. They can therefore also be checked headlessly:

python examples/sectioning/mesh_sections_and_clips.py --no-viewer
python examples/sectioning/brep_sections_and_clips.py --no-viewer

Python 3.14 and COMPAS Viewer 2.0.1

The shared examples/viewer.py helper contains a narrowly scoped compatibility adapter for a configuration-annotation issue in COMPAS Viewer 2.0.1 on Python 3.14. It changes only viewer configuration initialization and has no effect on collision calculations.

docs.title: brep_brep_contacts
docs.text:
brep_brep_contacts(
    a: Brep,
    b: Brep,
    tolerance: float = 1e-06,
    minimum_area: float = 0.1,
    deflection: float | None = None,
    contacttype: type[Contact] = Contact,
) -> list[Contact]

Compute all face-face contact interfaces between two breps.

Parameters:

  • a (Brep) –

    The source brep.

  • b (Brep) –

    The target brep.

  • tolerance (float, default: 1e-06 ) –

    Maximum deviation from the perfectly flat interface plane.

  • minimum_area (float, default: 0.1 ) –

    Minimum area of a "face-face" interface.

  • deflection (float | None, default: None ) –

    Linear deflection used to compute face overlaps.

  • contacttype (type[Contact], default: Contact ) –

    The contact class to use for the generated interfaces.

Returns:

  • list[Contact] –

    The detected contact interfaces.

Notes

For equilibrium calculations (e.g. with CRA), it is important that interface frames are aligned with the direction of the (interaction) edges on which they are stored.

This means that if the bestfit frame does not align with the normal of the base source frame, it will be inverted, such that it corresponds to whatever edge is created from this source to a target.

docs.title: mesh_mesh_contacts
docs.text:
mesh_mesh_contacts(
    a: Mesh,
    b: Mesh,
    tolerance: float = 1e-06,
    minimum_area: float = 0.1,
    contacttype: type[Contact] = Contact,
) -> list[Contact]

Compute all face-face contact interfaces between two meshes.

Parameters:

  • a (Mesh) –

    The source mesh.

  • b (Mesh) –

    The target mesh.

  • tolerance (float, default: 1e-06 ) –

    Maximum deviation from the perfectly flat interface plane.

  • minimum_area (float, default: 0.1 ) –

    Minimum area of a "face-face" interface.

  • contacttype (type[Contact], default: Contact ) –

    The contact class to use for the generated interfaces.

Returns:

  • list[Contact] –

    The detected contact interfaces.

Notes

For equilibrium calculations (e.g. with CRA), it is important that interface frames are aligned with the direction of the (interaction) edges on which they are stored.

This means that if the bestfit frame does not align with the normal of the base source frame, it will be inverted, such that it corresponds to whatever edge is created from this source to a target.
